title: PLL Fundamentals
intro: A phase-locked loop forces the phase of an oscillator to follow a reference.

items: Phase detector (PD) or phase/frequency detector (PFD): outputs a signal proportional to the phase difference.
VCO: integrates the control voltage into phase.
Optional divider by N in the feedback path.

blocks.text: In lock the VCO frequency is exactly N times the reference frequency and the phase error is constant (zero for a charge-pump PLL).

blocks.alt: Block diagram of a charge-pump phase-locked loop. The reference frequency enters a phase detector, followed by a charge pump, a loop filter and a voltage-controlled oscillator. The oscillator output is the loop output and also goes through a divide-by-N block back to the second input of the phase detector.
blocks.caption: A charge-pump PLL. The divider brings the VCO frequency down so it can be compared with the reference.

blocks.text: A PFD drives a charge pump that sources or sinks current Ip into a filter (R in series with C). The filter plus the VCO integrator give two integrators, so the phase error settles to zero. The loop behaves like a second-order system:

blocks.source:
w_n = sqrt( Ip * K_VCO / (2*pi * N * C1) )          zeta = (R1 / 2) * sqrt( Ip * K_VCO * C1 / (2*pi * N) )
Output frequency  f_out = N * f_ref

items: Loop bandwidth should be well below the reference frequency (a tenth or less) for stability and low ripple.
Larger bandwidth tracks and suppresses the VCO noise; smaller bandwidth filters the reference noise.
Non-ideal effects: charge-pump mismatch gives static phase offset, ripple on the control line gives reference spurs, and delays in the PFD cause a dead zone.

blocks.text: A DLL aligns delayed copies of a clock rather than an oscillator, so it has no phase accumulation and is unconditionally stable (first-order), used in memory interfaces. PLLs are used in clock synthesis, clock-data recovery and frequency synthesis in radios.

blocks.title: Frequency synthesis
blocks.text: f_ref = 10 MHz and N = 240. Find f_out. What N gives 2.45 GHz?

blocks.title: Loop dynamics
blocks.text: Ip = 100 uA, K_VCO = 2*pi * 500 MHz/V = 3.14e9 rad/s/V, N = 100, C1 = 10 pF. Find w_n and f_n.
solution: f_n = 7.07e6 / (2*pi) = 1.13 MHz, about a tenth of a 10 MHz reference, at the edge of the usual limit.
